beginner: Eggplant likes rich, well-drained soil that warms up well in the sun, since it is a heat-loving plant that hates cold, soggy ground. Mix in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting. If your soil is heavy clay or slow to warm, a sheet of black plastic or fabric mulch laid down before planting warms the soil and gives eggplant the head start it wants. Aim for soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged.
seasoned: Eggplant wants a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam rich in organic matter, and above all a soil that warms early and stays warm. As a heat-loving crop it sulks in cold, wet ground, so a sandy loam that warms quickly in spring suits it better than a heavy, slow-warming clay. Work 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting, and on heavy or cool soils many growers lay black plastic or fabric mulch to raise soil temperature and set transplants into warmer ground. Steady moisture in a soil that drains freely is the target, since soggy roots stall this warmth-demanding plant and invite the soilborne wilts it is prone to.

beginner: Eggplant likes slightly acidic soil, about pH 5.5 to 6.8, and a lot of garden soil is already close. The pH scale runs from acidic to alkaline, and this range is where eggplant takes up nutrients best. If your soil runs alkaline (common in the dry interior West), you may need to add sulfur before planting. An inexpensive soil test from your local extension office tells you where you stand.
seasoned: Eggplant grows best at a soil pH of about 5.5 to 6.8, with a sweet spot near 6.0 to 6.5 where the nutrients it needs stay most available. It tolerates a somewhat wider band, up to roughly 7.5, but uptake of iron, manganese, and other micronutrients tightens as the soil turns alkaline, showing up as yellowing between the veins of younger leaves. Alkaline soils common across the interior West often need sulfur worked in before planting; most Eastern and Midwestern soils sit naturally near the target. A simple soil test from your local extension office settles it before you plant.

beginner: Eggplant grows for a long time and likes steady feeding, but the timing matters. Mix a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the soil before you plant. Then wait: once the first little eggplants have set, feed with a nitrogen fertilizer, and again a few weeks later. Going heavy on fertilizer too early gives you a big leafy plant with few flowers, so save the feeding for after the fruit starts forming.
seasoned: Eggplant is a moderately heavy feeder over a long season. Work a complete fertilizer such as 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress with nitrogen once the first fruits have set and again three to four weeks later through the harvest. Hold the nitrogen back before fruit set, since too much early on drives leafy growth and few flowers; the time to push it is after the plant starts carrying fruit. Pair feeding with steady moisture, because fertilizer only helps a plant that is not also drought-stressed.

beginner: Your eggplant is setting fruit. Feed it now with a nitrogen fertilizer to keep it producing.
seasoned: Your eggplant has set its first fruit, time to side-dress with nitrogen to keep production going through the season.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then switch to a nitrogen feed once the fruit sets. Do not overdo the nitrogen early or you get all leaves and no eggplants.
seasoned: A complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting, then a nitrogen side-dress (for example calcium nitrate, 15.5-0-0) once fruit sets. Avoid heavy nitrogen before fruit set, which gives leaf at the expense of flowers.

beginner: Mix 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet (or a few inches of compost) into the soil before planting. Then, once fruit has set, scratch a nitrogen fertilizer into the soil a few inches out from each plant and water it in, repeating every three to four weeks.
seasoned: A common rate is 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet worked into the bed before transplanting, then a side-dress of about 0.5 pound of calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) per 100 square feet once the first fruits set, repeated every three to four weeks through harvest, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in.

beginner: The most useful eggplant companions help with its two biggest pests, flea beetles and Colorado potato beetles. Aromatic herbs and a ring of nasturtiums or marigolds can draw or shoo those pests away, and bush beans add a little nitrogen. The one rule that really matters is to keep eggplant away from tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes, which are all close relatives and share the same pests and soil diseases.
seasoned: Most eggplant companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested, and the ones worth acting on target its two signature problems: flea beetles and the Colorado potato beetle. Aromatic herbs and a border of nasturtium or marigold are the classic deflectors, drawing or repelling flea beetles and aphids off the crop, while bush beans both fix a little nitrogen and serve as a noted trap for the potato beetle. The single firmest rule is a rotation one: keep eggplant away from its Solanaceae relatives, tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes, which share its full pest and disease complex, including verticillium wilt and the flea beetle.

beginner: Bush beans add a little nitrogen to the soil and can lure Colorado potato beetles away from your eggplant. A good, traditional neighbor.
seasoned: Legumes fix a little nitrogen the long-feeding eggplant appreciates, and bush beans are a noted trap host for the Colorado potato beetle, helping pull it off the crop. A traditional, mechanistically plausible pairing rather than a trial-isolated one.

beginner: Nasturtiums are often grown near eggplant to lure flea beetles and aphids away from the crop. A helpful, low-risk neighbor.
seasoned: Often planted around solanaceous crops as a trap and deterrent for flea beetles and aphids, drawing them off the eggplant. Trap cropping is a documented principle, but the specific nasturtium-eggplant effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

beginner: Marigolds are a classic companion flower for eggplant, traditionally grown to help keep pests down. Mostly tradition, but a cheerful, low-risk choice.
seasoned: A long-standing companion tradition near eggplant; French marigold grown as a cover crop has documented nematode-suppressive effects, though the interplanted marigold-eggplant pest benefit is traditional rather than trial-isolated.

beginner: Strong-smelling herbs like thyme, oregano, and dill are traditionally planted near eggplant to help confuse pests like flea beetles. A pleasant, low-risk companion.
seasoned: Pungent herbs such as thyme, oregano, and dill are traditionally interplanted to confuse or repel flea beetles and other pests and to draw beneficial insects. The effect is plausible and habitat-based rather than trial-isolated for eggplant.

beginner: Keep eggplant away from tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes. They are all close relatives that share the same pests and soil diseases, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
seasoned: All are Solanaceae and share eggplant's full pest and disease complex, including flea beetle, Colorado potato beetle, verticillium and bacterial wilt, and the blights. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread the nightshades out and rotate them on at least a 3 to 4 year cycle.

beginner: Many gardeners keep fennel away from eggplant and most other vegetables, since it is said to stunt their growth. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
seasoned: A widely repeated caution that fennel inhibits the growth of many garden vegetables and is best kept to its own corner. There is no strong T1 mechanism for an eggplant-fennel antagonism, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

beginner: The leaves are peppered with lots of tiny round holes, as if hit by birdshot. It hits young plants hardest and can devastate seedlings. Touch the plant and you will see tiny dark beetles jump away.
seasoned: Tiny shot-hole punctures riddle the leaves, a scatter of small round holes that is the classic flea-beetle signature on eggplant. Damage is by far most severe on seedlings and young transplants, whose small leaf area a heavy infestation can shred or kill outright; established plants tolerate considerable feeding. Brush a plant and the small dark beetles spring away like fleas.

beginner: Small dark beetles that jump like fleas and chew tiny holes in the leaves. They are most active in spring and love eggplant, so they target young plants early in the season.
seasoned: Several Epitrix flea beetle species that feed on eggplant foliage, overwintering as adults in debris and emerging to attack the earliest, most vulnerable plants in spring. Eggplant is a strongly preferred host, and the beetles concentrate on it, which is why flea beetles are the defining early-season eggplant pest.

beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover until they are big and strong, then take it off when they flower. Setting out larger transplants helps them outgrow the damage. For heavy attacks on seedlings, an organic spray such as spinosad or a kaolin clay coating helps.
seasoned: Protect transplants with floating row cover until they are large and vigorous, removing it at flowering. Set out stout, well-hardened transplants rather than tiny seedlings so plants can outgrow the damage, and treat heavy early infestations with spinosad or kaolin clay. Mature plants rarely need treatment.

beginner: Cover plants early with row cover, set out larger transplants into warm soil so they grow quickly, and clear away weeds and old plant debris where the beetles hide over winter. A border of nasturtiums can lure them away.
seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, delay setting plants out until the soil and air are warm so they grow away fast, and clean up crop debris and weeds that harbor overwintering adults. A nasturtium or other trap planting at the bed edge can draw beetles off the crop.

beginner: Striped yellow-and-black beetles and plump red larvae with black spots eat the leaves, sometimes stripping a plant bare. Eggplant is one of their favorite foods. Check the undersides of leaves for clusters of orange-yellow eggs.
seasoned: Rounded yellow-and-black-striped adults and humpbacked, brick-red larvae with rows of black spots chew the leaves, and eggplant is a favorite host. Both stages feed voraciously and populations build fast, so an unmanaged infestation can defoliate plants and cut yield sharply. Look for clusters of orange-yellow eggs on leaf undersides.

beginner: A striped beetle whose larvae and adults both feed on eggplant and potato leaves. They overwinter in the soil, show up as plants get going, and multiply quickly through the summer.
seasoned: Leptinotarsa decemlineata, a Solanaceae specialist that prefers potato and eggplant. Adults overwinter in the soil and nearby debris and move in as plants establish; left alone they go through multiple generations a season and quickly resist many insecticides, making non-chemical control important.

beginner: Pick the beetles, larvae, and egg clusters off by hand and drop them in soapy water, checking every day or two. Squash the orange egg clusters under the leaves. For heavy infestations, an organic spray such as spinosad or Bt (the tenebrionis strain) works on the young larvae.
seasoned: In a home garden, hand-pick adults, larvae, and egg clusters daily into soapy water, which keeps small plantings clean. Crush egg masses on leaf undersides, and where pressure is high apply spinosad or Bacillus thuringiensis var. tenebrionis to young larvae. Rotating away from last year's nightshade bed cuts the overwintered population.

beginner: Do not plant eggplant where potatoes, tomatoes, or eggplant grew last year, since the beetles come up from the soil there. Cover young plants with row cover, and a thick straw mulch makes it harder for the beetles to reach them.
seasoned: Rotate eggplant well away from where potatoes, tomatoes, or eggplant grew last year, since the overwintered adults emerge near old hosts. Row cover on young plants excludes the colonizers, and a thick straw mulch hinders the adults that walk in from the soil.

beginner: Tiny soft green or black insects gather on new growth and the undersides of leaves, making them curl and yellow, often with a sticky film and black mold. They can also spread plant viruses.
seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often green peach aphid, cluster on growing tips and leaf undersides, causing leaves to curl, pucker, and yellow, with sticky honeydew and sooty mold following. Beyond direct feeding, aphids transmit mosaic and other viruses that mottle and distort the foliage.

beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that multiply quickly in warm weather, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer. The sticky honeydew they leave grows black mold.
seasoned: Several aphid species, predominantly green peach aphid, that suck sap and reproduce rapidly in warm weather, building up fast on soft, over-fertilized growth. The honeydew they excrete fosters sooty mold that shades the leaves.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control.

beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, and let helpful insects do their work instead of spraying everything.
seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Reflective mulch deters aphids from young plants.

beginner: The leaves look dusty or speckled with tiny yellow dots, and in bad cases you see fine webbing underneath. The leaves can bronze and dry out. Mites love hot, dry weather.
seasoned: Fine yellow stippling speckles the leaves, which may bronze, dry, and drop, and in bad infestations fine webbing appears on leaf undersides. Two-spotted spider mites thrive in hot, dry weather, exactly the conditions eggplant is grown in, so mite pressure often peaks in midsummer.

beginner: Tiny mites, almost too small to see, that feed on the undersides of leaves and thrive in hot, dry, dusty conditions. They build up fast in summer.
seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related mites that feed on the lower leaf surfaces with piercing mouthparts. Populations explode in heat and drought and on dusty, water-stressed plants, and can build quickly on eggplant in summer.

beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water every day for a week, then follow up with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil if needed. Keeping plants well watered helps, since stressed plants are hit hardest.
seasoned: Spray the leaf undersides with a strong jet of water repeatedly to disrupt colonies, then apply insecticidal soap or horticultural oil to the undersides, repeating every few days. Keeping plants well watered and raising humidity discourages mites; predatory mites help under heavy pressure.

beginner: Keep plants well watered in hot weather, hose dust off the leaves now and then, and avoid spraying broad insecticides that kill the helpful bugs that eat mites.
seasoned: Keep plants well watered in hot weather, since drought-stressed plants are most vulnerable, avoid dusty conditions, and avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill the predators holding mites in check.

beginner: The tops of the leaves look pale and stippled, and underneath you find dark sticky specks and small insects with lacy-looking wings. Bad infestations brown and curl the leaves.
seasoned: Leaves develop a pale, yellow-stippled or bleached look on top, while the undersides carry dark, varnish-like specks of excrement and the small, lacy-winged adults and spiny nymphs. Heavy feeding browns and curls the foliage and can stunt the plant, and lace bugs are fairly eggplant-specific.

beginner: A small flat insect with lacy wings that feeds in groups on the undersides of eggplant leaves, sucking out the juices. It is most active in warm weather.
seasoned: The eggplant lace bug (Gargaphia solani), a true bug that feeds in colonies on leaf undersides with piercing-sucking mouthparts. It overwinters in debris and is most damaging in warm weather, with several generations a season.

beginner: Check the undersides of the leaves and spray any colonies directly with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, making sure to coat underneath. Pick off and destroy the most badly affected leaves.
seasoned: Scout leaf undersides early and treat colonies directly with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, which reach the soft nymphs, covering the undersides thoroughly and repeating as needed. Remove and destroy the worst-infested leaves.

beginner: Clear away old plants at the end of the season, move eggplant to a new spot each year, and check the undersides of the lower leaves early so you catch the bugs before they spread.
seasoned: Clean up crop debris at season's end to remove overwintering sites, rotate eggplant, and scout the undersides of lower leaves from early in the season so colonies are caught while small.

beginner: Whole leaves vanish overnight, leaving just the veins, with dark droppings on the leaves below. The cause is a large green caterpillar that hides against the stems, easier to spot by its droppings than by sight.
seasoned: Large sections of leaf, and sometimes whole shoots, are stripped down to the veins overnight, with dark pellet droppings on the leaves below. The culprits are big green tomato or tobacco hornworms, up to four inches long, that blend into the stems and are easiest to find by their frass.

beginner: Big green caterpillars, the young of large moths, that feed on eggplant and tomato leaves mostly in mid to late summer. Even a few can strip a lot of foliage.
seasoned: Tomato and tobacco hornworms, the larvae of large sphinx moths, which feed on solanaceous foliage including eggplant from midsummer on. A few caterpillars can do conspicuous damage given their size.

beginner: Pick the caterpillars off by hand and drop them in soapy water. If you find one covered in small white capsules, leave it, those are parasitic wasps that will do the work for you. An organic Bt spray works on the smaller caterpillars.
seasoned: Hand-pick the caterpillars, which is effective in a home garden, and apply Bacillus thuringiensis to younger larvae where numbers are high. Leave any hornworm studded with white parasitic-wasp cocoons in place, since the wasps will kill it and breed more.

beginner: Turn the soil at the end of the season to destroy the pupae, watch for droppings and missing leaves from midsummer, and welcome the helpful wasps that attack hornworms.
seasoned: Till the soil in fall to destroy overwintering pupae, scout for frass and stripped leaves from midsummer, and encourage the parasitic wasps and other natural enemies that keep hornworms in check.

beginner: Leaves turn yellow and wilt, often on one side of the plant first, then brown and drop while the plant stunts. Cut a wilting stem and you may see brown streaks inside. It is the most common serious eggplant disease.
seasoned: Lower and outer leaves yellow, often in a wedge or one-sided pattern, then wilt, brown, and drop, working upward as the plant stunts and fails to size its fruit. A cut through a wilting stem shows tan-to-brown streaking in the water-conducting tissue. It is the most common and damaging eggplant disease in much of the country.

beginner: A soil fungus that infects the roots and blocks the plant's water pipes, so it wilts even when watered. It lives in the soil for years and attacks many crops, especially the nightshade family.
seasoned: Verticillium dahliae, a soilborne fungus that infects the roots and clogs the vascular system, so the plant wilts despite moist soil. It persists in soil for years as resting structures, has a wide host range across the Solanaceae and many other crops, and is favored by cool-to-moderate soil temperatures.

beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. The real answer is prevention: rotate your crops and choose resistant or grafted plants next time.
seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy affected plants. Management is preventive and centered on rotation and resistant or grafted plants, since the fungus cannot be eradicated from infested soil by home-garden means.

beginner: Plant eggplant in soil with no recent history of the disease, rotate away from tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes, and look for resistant or grafted plants. Keeping plants healthy with steady water and feeding helps them cope.
seasoned: Do not plant eggplant where verticillium-susceptible crops (tomato, pepper, potato, eggplant, and many others) have grown, rotate on a long cycle, choose tolerant varieties or grafted plants on resistant rootstock, and keep plants vigorous with steady water and balanced feeding. Solarizing infested beds can lower inoculum.

beginner: Pale sunken spots on the fruit spread quickly into soft, rotting patches, and the disease can also spot the leaves and rot the stem near the base. It is worst in warm, wet weather and later in the season.
seasoned: Pale, sunken spots appear on the fruit that rapidly enlarge to soft, spongy, rotting areas, sometimes shrinking the fruit into a dry mummy; the disease also causes grayish leaf spots and a collar rot that can break young stems an inch or two above the soil line. It is most damaging in warm, wet weather and toward fall.

beginner: A fungus carried on seed and in old plant debris that spreads in warm, wet weather. It can come in on infected seed, so starting clean matters.
seasoned: Phomopsis vexans, a fungus that is both soil- and seedborne and overwinters on crop debris. Warm, humid conditions and splashing water spread it, and infected seed or volunteer debris often starts an outbreak, so clean seed and rotation are central to control.

beginner: Pick off and throw away infected fruit and plants right away. Keep the leaves and fruit dry by watering at the soil, and use a labeled fungicide if it is spreading. Rotted fruit cannot be saved.
seasoned: Remove and destroy infected fruit and plants promptly to limit spread, and where the disease is active apply a labeled fungicide, keeping foliage and fruit as dry as possible. There is no rescue for badly rotted fruit.

beginner: Use clean seed and healthy transplants, do not plant eggplant in the same spot for about four years, water at the soil instead of over the leaves, and clean up old plants at the end of the season.
seasoned: Start with clean, treated, or resistant seed and disease-free transplants, rotate eggplant out of the bed for about four years, water at the soil rather than overhead, mulch to limit splash, space for airflow, and remove crop debris at season's end.

beginner: The plant wilts and collapses suddenly even though the soil is wet, without much yellowing first. If you cut the stem near the base, the inside looks brown, and a cut stem held in a glass of water gives off milky strands. It is mainly a problem in the hot, wet South.
seasoned: Individual leaves, then whole plants, wilt and collapse suddenly even though the soil is moist, with little of the yellowing that precedes verticillium. Cut low on the stem and the pith is discolored reddish-brown; suspended in clear water, a cut stem streams milky bacterial ooze. It is most serious in hot, wet soils of the South.

beginner: A soil bacterium that gets into the roots and blocks the plant's water flow, so it wilts fast. It lives in warm, wet soil and spreads in water and on tools.
seasoned: Ralstonia solanacearum, a soilborne bacterium that invades the roots and plugs the vascular tissue. It survives in soil and infected debris, spreads in water and on tools, and is favored by high soil temperature and moisture, so it is most damaging in warm, wet regions.

beginner: There is no cure, so pull and destroy any plant that wilts from it, and clean your tools. The real fix is prevention next season.
seasoned: There is no cure; remove and destroy wilted plants promptly to limit spread, and disinfect tools. Because it persists in soil, management is preventive, through rotation, resistant or grafted plants, and improved drainage.

beginner: Do not plant eggplant where tomatoes, potatoes, or eggplant grew in the last three years, improve drainage in wet spots, and look for resistant or grafted plants if this disease is common where you live.
seasoned: Avoid planting eggplant where tomato, potato, or eggplant grew in the previous three years, choose resistant varieties or graft onto resistant rootstock in problem areas, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil or working among wet plants.

beginner: Dark, wet-looking patches appear on the stems, leaves, or fruit, and the plant can wilt and die quickly. The fruit can rot, sometimes with white fuzzy growth. It strikes in warm, wet, poorly drained ground.
seasoned: Dark, water-soaked lesions and streaking develop on stems, leaves, or fruit, and a plant can collapse and die rapidly once the stem is girdled. Fruit rots with a firm, sometimes white-cottony decay. It flares in warm, wet, poorly drained conditions and after heavy rain or flooding.

beginner: A mold-like disease that lives in wet soil and spreads in splashing water, attacking plants in warm, soggy conditions. It moves fast once it starts.
seasoned: Phytophthora species (such as P. capsici and P. nicotianae), water molds that thrive in saturated soil and spread in splashing and running water. They survive in soil and debris and move fast in warm, wet weather, especially on heavy or poorly drained ground.

beginner: Pull and destroy affected plants and fruit, and fix the drainage. There is no good home cure once it takes hold, so prevention is what matters.
seasoned: Remove and destroy affected plants and fruit promptly, and improve drainage immediately. There is no effective home-garden cure once plants collapse, so control is preventive and drainage-based.

beginner: Plant on raised beds or mounds so water drains away, avoid wet low spots, water at the soil, and keep fruit off soggy ground. Rotate away from peppers, tomatoes, and squash.
seasoned: Plant on raised, well-drained beds or hills, avoid low spots that stay wet, water at the soil rather than overhead, mulch to limit splash, rotate away from solanaceous and cucurbit crops, and keep fruit up off saturated soil.

beginner: Give eggplant about 1 inch of water a week, more when it is hot and dry. Water deeply rather than a little every day. Plants in pots dry out much faster and may need checking daily in summer.
seasoned: Aim for about 1 inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation, more in heat or on sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. As a heat-loving plant grown through the hottest part of the year, eggplant transpires heavily in summer, and container plants dry out far faster still.

beginner: About 1 inch of water a week, soaking the soil down 6 to 8 inches so the roots grow deep. Keep it even: letting the soil go bone-dry and then flooding it stresses the plant and makes flowers drop.
seasoned: Around 1 inch per week is the working range, leaning higher during flowering and fruit set, wetting the soil to a depth of at least 6 to 8 inches so the roots follow the moisture down. Even, deep watering is what sizes well-shaped fruit; letting the soil swing from dry to soaked stresses the plant and drops blossoms.

beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, with a soaker hose or by holding the hose at the base. Keeping the leaves dry helps prevent disease. If you must use a sprinkler, do it in the morning so the leaves dry off by evening. Mulch helps keep the soil evenly moist and warm.
seasoned: Water at the base with a soaker hose or drip line, keeping the foliage as dry as possible, since wet leaves favor the leaf spots and fruit rots eggplant is prone to. If overhead watering is unavoidable, do it in the morning so leaves dry before evening. A layer of mulch buffers soil moisture and warmth and blocks soil-borne spores from splashing onto the lower leaves.

beginner: If the lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or stems and fruit go soft and rotten, it is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and soft, rotting stems or fruit point to overwatering or poor drainage. Saturated soil starves the roots of oxygen and invites the Phytophthora and bacterial wilts eggplant is susceptible to, especially on heavy ground.

beginner: Some midday wilting in hot weather is normal and passes by evening. Leaves that stay wilted mean the plant is too dry, and drought while it is flowering causes dropped blossoms and small, bitter fruit.
seasoned: Midday wilting that recovers overnight is common in heat and not alarming, but leaves that stay limp and dull signal real drought. Drought stress during flowering and fruit set shows up as dropped blossoms and small, misshapen, sometimes bitter fruit.

beginner: Keep the seed tray evenly damp and warm while the seeds come up. Eggplant likes it warm and sprouts slowly, so do not let the surface dry out.
seasoned: Keep the seed-starting mix evenly moist and warm through germination; eggplant is heat-loving and slow to sprout, and the surface must not dry mid-emergence.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp, not soggy. Let the top begin to dry before watering again.
seasoned: Grow seedlings on under lights with even, moderate moisture, easing off between waterings so the mix never stays saturated.

beginner: Soak the plant in well when you set it out, then keep the soil evenly moist as it takes hold. Mulch keeps the moisture and warmth steady.
seasoned: Water in thoroughly at transplant, then hold even moisture at the base as this heat-lover establishes; mulch to buffer soil moisture and warmth.

beginner: Keep watering steady once flowers open, about 1 inch a week soaked in deep. If the soil swings from dry to soaked, the flowers drop off and you get fewer fruit.
seasoned: Eggplant wants a steady 1 inch a week soaked 6 to 8 inches deep, leaning higher through flowering and fruit set. Even moisture sets fruit and prevents blossom drop; unlike peppers, eggplant is not prone to blossom-end rot, so the failure mode of dry-wet swings here is dropped blossoms, not fruit rot.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while the fruit fill out. Letting it dry hard and then soaking it gives small, bitter, oddly shaped fruit, so keep the water steady.
seasoned: Fruit set through sizing is the water-critical stretch: steady, deep moisture sizes well-shaped fruit, while a dry-then-flooded swing gives small, bitter, misshapen fruit. Keep the ripening fruit up off wet ground and the soil evenly moist.

beginner: Keep watering evenly while you pick. Eggplant keeps making new fruit, and steady water keeps them tender instead of small and bitter.
seasoned: Keep even moisture through the picking weeks; eggplant keeps flowering and setting fruit as you harvest, and steady water keeps the later fruit from turning small and bitter.

beginner: Watering the soil instead of the leaves is the best thing you can do for eggplant. It keeps the plant hydrated without encouraging leaf and fruit disease.
seasoned: Base watering is the most useful habit for eggplant, because the same plant that wants steady moisture is also prone to leaf spots and fruit and root rots. Keep water on the soil, air moving through the leaves, and the ripening fruit up off wet ground.

beginner: The most important time to keep eggplant evenly watered is when it is flowering and setting fruit. Uneven water now causes dropped flowers and small, bitter fruit, so aim for steady moisture.
seasoned: The water-critical stretch runs from flowering through fruit set and sizing. Steady moisture here sets and fills well-shaped fruit, while swings between dry and saturated soil drop blossoms and give small, bitter, misshapen fruit. Keep it even once the plant is carrying fruit.

beginner: Pick eggplant while it is young and shiny, not when it is biggest. A ready eggplant has firm flesh and a bright, glossy skin, and when you press the side with your thumb the dent springs back. If the skin looks dull instead of shiny, you waited too long: the inside will be seedy, spongy, and bitter. Harvest large oval types when they are firm and glossy and slimmer Asian types at finger or hot-dog size. Cut the fruit off with scissors or a knife, leaving a little stem on, instead of pulling, because the stems are tough and sometimes prickly. Keep picking every few days, since taking the fruit young keeps the plant making more.
